title: DC Blockchain Summit 2026: Senator Bill Hagerty & Chainlink Labs' Ben Sherwin
description:
Ben Sherwin, General Counsel at Chainlink Labs, joins U.S. Senator Bill Hagerty at the DC Blockchain Summit 2026 to discuss the GENIUS Act, the regulatory environment for digital assets, and more.

#Blockchain #Crypto #Chainlink #Web3 #DCBlockchainSummit #DigitalAssets

asr.full_text: Thanks for being with me today, certainly. Certainly really appreciate it. You know, I find that a lot of people in this room I have my own story coming to the space and have gotten interested and I came from the financial markets like you did. And in terms of where the origin of your championing of modernization of financial systems? Where was that borne out of? Financial systems in general, I have to go back, to start with the start of my career. I started at a place called the Boston Consulting Group when it was much smaller than it is today. I did a great deal of work in the financial services arena and also in the payments area. I think that helped me understand and appreciate the mechanics, if you will. great deal of work in the financial services arena and also in the payments area. I think that that helped me understand and appreciate the mechanics, if you will, and the guts of the system, so to speak, as as it existed in the traditional legacy system, and then as a venture and private equity investor later in life, the difficulties that one encounters, particularly if you're funding and supporting and leading a smaller company typically doing business with much larger companies. The notion of a self-executing contract was absolutely one of the most attractive things I've seen because any of you in the audience know this. You're the smaller company dealing with one much larger. The odds of you completing the contract and getting re-traded at the end of the day? Pretty, aye, right and you know having contracts that are agreed on the front end and executed as they're performed that that would have been a blessing to me in my career think about the brain damage I went through renegotiating things at the end on a fairly regular basis, but there's another twist that took place in my career I I left the private sector to go serves as US Ambassador to Japan in 2017 and if you remember what things are like in 2017 in that arena you had Kim Jaegin bragging about how big his button was launching intercontinental ballistic missiles over Japan detonating thermonuclear weapons, and we were doing everything we could to block the North Koreans from getting access to hard currency. The United States, a number of you will know this as well, the United States has more U.S. military stations in Japan than anyplace else in the world. A large intel operation. That's for a reason, it's a very tough neighborhood out there. And you got not only North Korea, but you've got Russia and China right at your doorstep. So I spent a tremendous amount of time focused on the North Korea issue and how to stop them from continuing to fund and fuel their nuclear ambitions. We literally were blocking ship-to-ship trans, you know, ship movements of coal from one North Korean ship to a Chinese ship, you know, where we might be blocking three, five, six million dollars. We'd have the Secretary of State on the phone to a foreign minister of some other country saying, don't hire North Korean guest workers. That might add up to $17-$20 million. Then, one day I come into my office in the morning, and above the fold and one of the Japanese newspapers, headline, heist at coin check in dollars, over half a billion dollars stolen in one night. I calls on my team. I said are you guys tracking this? Sir, we're tracking it, but we can't get and I'm going to use the wrong word. We can't get the malware from the Japanese government, loss of face, difficult to deal with. I had to quote malware within an hour. We had a back to the states. The analysis came back overnight, definitely a state actor. My suspicion was probably Lazarus Group out of North Korea. We never were able to pin it for sure because the better they are the fewer fingerprints they leave. But I saw this, and I thought this is terrible. You know, we've got a real problem here in terms of the use of these digital currencies by state actors that don't have our best interest at heart, and then I watched what happened after that. And as that digital currency started to come into the mainstream we started catching people that were involved in, and with the proper authorities, and I wanna emphasize this, but with the proper authorities there is a lot you could do in terms of dealing with illicit finance and we have been dealing with illicit finance I remind my colleagues since biblical times and and there's always been a great concern among among folks that are that are very focused on national security issues that we not allow in any bad actors to have any access to fund their operations well just because the currency is digital or because because it's paper, or it could be something bartered—I don't think we should let that block an entire area of innovation. And that's where I found the United States, when I came to the United States Senate in 2021. There was a huge resistance to any digital assets, and if you think about the way the SEC was being run under Gary Gensler, Uncertainty was the name of the game. I remember just asking him to define whether Bitcoin was a security or a commodity. The answer was, well it depends, it depends. And the uncertainty then led to regulation by enforcement actions, and what I saw was innovation moving offshore, and I'm sure a number of people in this room definitely remember those days it wasn't long ago when the best developers were telling me well we're going to Portugal or wherever it might be, but it wasn't in the United States. That's you know, you have something like Sam Bankman freeing his fraud, manifested itself off shore, that's exactly what can happen. When I saw the spreadsheet he was using to run his business, I've lived in the financial world, I was on the board of directors for years for RJ O'Brien for the largest futures and commodities merchant in Chicago, I understand about customer seg, they weren't segregated into funds at all. Is this very easy to predict if it had been regulated it would've never happened. And frankly, what I hope people can do to support this is to say, Oh, I understand about customer seg. they weren't segregated in the funds at all. You could is this very easy to predict it if it had been regulated, it would have never happened. In fact, the one regulated component of FTX is still existing. It still works. It was everything offshore that fell apart. So it was very clear. We need to get this innovation back onshore. We need to support it in a way that allows that innovation to thrive here in America because the efficiencies that it can offer whether it be just in fixing the payment rails and we can go into that with respect to stable coins or the innovation it will create of whether its self fulfilling contracts and you can go on and on about what it can provide I want to see that happen here. And we'll talk about market structure in a minute, I think, which will bring it to some regulatory clarity to the fore. But as we struggle now to get that across the line, you led the way on genius and really changed the game for the industry. Can you talk a little bit about what lessons you learned in developing that bipartisan momentum to get it across the line when it's so important to this country? in developing that bipartisan momentum to get it across the line when it's so important to this country? Certainly, the GNUS Act brought to the fore a deep philosophical divide. On the one hand, decentralization, and I would align that with liberty. On the other hand, heavy centralization and central control. I would align that with operations like chokepoint, chokepoint 2.0, the ability to control all financial transactions. And that philosophical divide manifested itself the day we brought the Genius Act to the banking committee for a vote. And the night before, I would say it was about 1158 p.m. as I recall The ranking member of the Senate banking committee Elizabeth Warren Even though the text had been out we've been asking for amendments, etc for months We got 84 amendments that night all designed to destroy the the bill and for four hours I went back and forth with the ranking member in a polite, respectful, and professional manner. It was almost like a tennis match, she'd send one over that, I'd send it back. Here's how it won't work. And after four hours, I didn't know how the vote was gonna shake out. But, as I watched the vote transpire, Senator Warren was able to hold five Democrats with her, and five Democrats came with me. It came out of the Senate Banking Committee the most bipartisan bill that has come out of the Senate Banking Committee in over a decade. That, I thought was a huge victory. President Biden- Yeah, let's have applause there. Mr. Now it didn't last long. Senator Warren's very effective. And I don't know what she said, but when we brought the bill to the floor, the process is called cloture. You've got to vote. You need 60 votes to quote, open the debate on the bill and every Democrat voted against it including my co-sponsors. They were, I'm sorry and and everyone came out and voted against it. And I went to a local community center and I said I wanted to vote against it including my Cosponsors they go I'm sorry And everyone came out and voted against it. And I went to John Thun the Senate majority leader and I said John I need a week. And it took me a little a bit longer than a week maybe 10 days, but just chipping away meeting with members across the aisle working through it. This gets to your point I think, of just trying to explain, here is what it is we're trying to do. And thankfully, having members willing to listen to me on this. And I think industry helped. There was a lot of industry outreach on both sides of the aisle. And a lot of education took place on both sides of the aisle. And the stable coin legislation, if you just think about the benefits of it those in the industry will understand this immediately, but I was able to explain to my colleagues that in doing this we're taking a clunky process that was designed back in the 70s and 80s one that takes five to ten days to close we're going to move that to something almost instantaneous as we go to the blockchain so if you think about counterparty risk if you're waiting five to ten days the other side of the trade could go bankrupt that's not a good that's not a good outcome if you think about currency risk let's say it's an overseas transaction with an instantaneous closing you're not worried about massive currency risk you're waiting ten days you're in waiting seven days whatever the number you could have pretty significant movements in the currency that risk goes away and by the way and this also where I got a lot of resistance you're taking capital that was otherwise tied up and float and you're putting it back into the economy what's not to like about that, well everybody likes it except those that were getting the float and the interest in the float. So, there you can imagine where a lot of resistance arose but we worked through all of that as well. And over time day by day with a lot of engagement a lot of a lot of work together we were able to get to 60 was not hard to get to 68 but to get that 59th and 60th very very difficult because again the ranking member was opposed to this heavily opposed to it again the decentralized nature is something that that I think is from a philosophical standpoint just completely counter uh you know to someone that wants to see a central bank digital currency and that type of construct this is this is not the way to go and that argument didn't prevail with 68 votes we passed the stablecoin act the president signed it and it was a really fun signing ceremony ceremony. When he read the bill and talked about the Genius Act it was the punchline I was expecting. And they named that after me. Tom Bilyeu, Vice President of the United States, Well, you know, thank you for your efforts on that and it really is a good, good day for America. It's, now the hard work is starts with implementation and the modernization of the payment rails. You know, and you've pointed out that, you know, it needs to happen in a certain way because, you know, you saw from Japan the North Koreans went along these lines. What's your vision of implementation, where you wanted to see it go? Is it just more competition, or is it just more sanctity and soundness? How are you thinking about that problem? So I think if you look at the design of the legislation what we've required is that a stablecoin a genius compliant stable coin has got to be backed dollar-for-dollar by US Treasury's short-term US Treasury securities or cash that's the safest instrument you could possibly have and we created the bankruptcy protection so that the stable coin is not captured. But if an issuer were to go bankrupt, this avoids that whole bankruptcy process. So those treasuries that are set aside for that will go to that. So it's an extraordinarily safe instrument. It can't be rehypothecated to bank and take a deposit and loan it out. An issuer of a stablecoin cannot do that so does not have that type of risk at all it's a hundred percent reserved in its 100% reserve with the safest possible collateral so it is a very special vehicle and the design of it is to create again an incredibly efficient payment system and in getting this rails design is going to be within the purview of the executive branch to do the administration. The OCC has put out its first round of, you know, put out its first draft I should say and they're expecting comments by early May. And I would encourage everybody in the industry here to look at it carefully and send your comments back because it's not set in stone, what what comes out. But what they're trying to do is put a stake in the ground so they can then get industry input to make sure that we do get it right. But I hope that people will look at that, participants in the industry will look at it and make certain that my overarching goals at least are met, and that is that the innovation and the opportunity to innovate remains, that we create efficiency. We create security in the system. And we create the most efficient clearing mechanism and the most efficient digital currency in the world so that the dollar remains the reserve currency of the world and that people all over the world want to use our digital dollars to transact. And as we look at market structure now, which is from the counterpoint to using these stable coin rails to improve on our financial system, how is that fight going from your perspective? Some of your colleagues are making news with predictions. I don't know if you feel comfortable in terms of timing making predictions on that. Given my role, I'd be very reluctant to start speculating on that, because I think anything I say is going to be headline worthy. I'll just say this. I spoke with Chairman Tim Scott just before coming over here. He and I are very aligned. In terms of prioritizing this and getting to it as soon as we reasonably can. And I think that timeline is denominated in weeks not months or it's in the near future we have issues before us we just passed the road to housing act through the Senate last week that opens that opens the aperture in the Banking Committee a lot of people in this room are dealing with the government for the first time and your your time is very valuable. Your staff's time is very valuable. Do you, any advice about how to engage with your staff and do it efficiently? Because I think you do want to hear from people. What's the best way for people to engage with your So Matt Benoit is here. I can't see because the lights are in my eyes, but if Matt can raise his hand he may be Backstage Matt is on my Staff right now and here with me today Matt has a team working with him in my Senate Office But as you mentioned a number of my alumni are over in the Treasury Department Several of them Senate confirmed which means they have large teams working for them They're at the Commerce Department at the SEC at the CFTC their their Hagerty alumni throughout that Network and all of them are very dialed in and engaged to this issue as well as the team at the White House against some people that mom my staff are over on the White House team they're working for David Sachs and Patrick wit so I would encourage you to engage, particularly right now with the OCC because they put out the first draft of the regulation, so please engage with them. Feel free to engage with the White House, with the officials, predominantly at Treasury on this as well and always know that my door's open with my staff. And so, I think, time for one last question. You, you're a Vanderbilt alum, I believe, and Vanderbilt's in the NCAA tournament, so I'd be remiss to not ask you how do you think they're gonna do this year? I was, I was just at a game a couple Saturday afternoons ago with my family. The energy is outstanding. I love seeing Vanderbilt's athletic program advance. We have a great new chancellor but we've extended his contract. I don't think I could get into Vanderbilt today. I was certainly lucky to get to attend when I did, but I think the prospects are very bright for Vanderbilt's basketball team and everyone. We've had a great baseball team for years. Coach Corbin is one of the best coaches in the nation in baseball. The football team has done a fantastic job in a lot of the smaller sports, the so-called Olympic Sports also thrive at Vanderbilt too, so if any of you have teenagers, kids in high school, I do. I have a junior in high school, I have three more that are already in college. But it would be a great place to look to send your child to school. It's a nice advertisement for Vanderbilt University certainly. And I appreciate my alma mater and I would also say there's somebody else I appreciate, too, that can't be here. And that's Angela Allsop Rooks. She called me earlier today, and she sends her apologies. She had a family emergency that arose, but she and I work very closely. She's a Democrat from Maryland. We work very closely on this legislation. She's working with me on what we call the Main Street Depositors Act. That's to deal with what we saw a real issue that emerged after the Silicon Valley bank failure with with asset runs from sort of you know large non and non intersparing transaction accounts that exist at small and medium sized banks these are you know the biggest employer in your community might have a five or ten million dollar payroll account that they're running every two weeks and they don't that it's not bearing interest it's not a savings account per se but we're trying to increase the FDIC insurance on that narrow slice because those with accounts the accounts they got poached and that fled to the Jeesons the largest banks because they're perceived just too big to fail and they have the implicit guarantee of the government that's an imbalance that dot Frank created that we're trying to rectify an angel and I are working on that that's great and I are working on that That's great and thank you for bringing that up it's very important Thank you so much for your time it's been fantastic and thank you for all you've done for America And thanks for all the great input that we've had from the industry here too We're making real progress Thank you

You know, I find that a lot of people in this room I have my own story coming to the space and have gotten interested and I came from the financial markets like you did. I think that helped me understand and appreciate the mechanics, if you will. great deal of work in the financial services arena and also in the payments area. The notion of a self-executing contract was absolutely one of the most attractive things I've seen because any of you in the audience know this. You're the smaller company dealing with one much larger. The odds of you completing the contract and getting re-traded at the end of the day? Pretty, aye, right and you know having contracts that are agreed on the front end and executed as they're

performed that that would have been a blessing to me in my career think about the brain damage I went through renegotiating things at the end on a fairly regular basis, but there's another twist that took place in my career I I left the private sector to go serves as US Ambassador to Japan in 2017 and if you remember what things are like in 2017 in that arena you had Kim Jaegin bragging about how big his button was launching intercontinental ballistic missiles over Japan detonating thermonuclear weapons, and we were doing everything we could to block the North Koreans from getting access to hard currency. The United States, a number of you will know this as well, the United States has more U.S. military stations in Japan than anyplace else in the world. A large intel operation. That's for a reason, it's a very tough neighborhood out there. And you got not only North Korea, but you've got Russia and China right at your doorstep. So I spent a tremendous amount of time focused on the North Korea issue and how to stop them from continuing to fund and fuel their nuclear ambitions. We literally were blocking ship-to-ship trans, you know, ship movements of coal from one North Korean ship to a Chinese ship, you know, where we might be blocking three, five, six million dollars. We'd have the Secretary of State on the phone to a foreign minister of some other country saying, don't hire North Korean guest workers. That might add up to $17-$20 million. check in dollars, over half a billion dollars stolen in one night. I calls on my team. I said are you guys tracking this? Sir, we're tracking it, but we can't get and I'm going to use the wrong word. We can't get the malware from the Japanese government, loss of face, difficult to deal with. I had to quote malware within an hour. We had a back to the states. The analysis came back overnight, definitely a state actor. My suspicion was probably Lazarus Group out of North Korea. President Biden- Yeah, let's have applause there. Mr. Now it didn't last long. Senator Warren's very effective. members willing to listen to me on this. And I think industry helped. There was a lot of industry outreach on both sides of the aisle. And a lot of education took place on both sides of the aisle. So, there you can imagine where a lot of resistance arose but we worked through all of that as well. 59th and 60th very very difficult because again the ranking member was opposed to this heavily opposed to it again the decentralized nature is something that that I think is from a philosophical standpoint just completely counter uh you know to someone that wants to see a central bank digital currency and that type of construct this is this is not the way to go and that argument didn't prevail with 68 votes we passed the stablecoin act the president signed it and it was a really fun signing ceremony ceremony. When he read the bill and talked about the Genius Act it was the punchline I was expecting. And they named that after me. Tom Bilyeu, Vice President of the United States, Well, you know, thank you for your efforts on that and it really is a good, good day for America. It's, now the hard work is starts with implementation and the modernization of the payment rails. You know, and you've pointed out that, you know, it needs to happen in a certain way because, you know, you saw from Japan the North Koreans went along these lines. What's your vision of implementation, where you wanted to see it go? Is it just more competition, or is it just more sanctity and soundness? How are you thinking about that problem? So I think if you look at the design of the legislation what we've required is that a stablecoin a genius compliant stable coin has got to be backed dollar-for-dollar by US Treasury's short-term US Treasury securities or cash that's the safest instrument you could possibly have and we created the bankruptcy protection so that the stable coin is not captured. But if

an issuer were to go bankrupt, this avoids that whole bankruptcy process. So those treasuries that are set aside for that will go to that. So it's an extraordinarily safe instrument. It can't be rehypothecated to bank and take a deposit and loan it out. An issuer of a stablecoin cannot do that so does not have that type of risk at all it's a hundred percent reserved in its 100% reserve with the safest possible collateral so it is a very special vehicle and the design of it is to create again an incredibly efficient payment system and in getting this rails design is going to be within the purview of the executive branch to do the administration.
